title: Psalm 126: Those Who Sow in Tears
summary: The people remember the day the LORD restored Zion's fortunes, when joy seemed too good to be real and even the nations said God had done great things for them. Then they pray for restoration again, like desert streams filling after rain, and hold on to the promise that those who sow in tears will come home with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves.
story: Psalm 126 stands at the center of the Songs of Ascents in feeling if not in number. After the trust of Psalm 125, it looks back on a great restoration and forward to one still needed. Its two halves hold together two things every generation of God's people knows: that God has acted, and that the work is not finished. The psalm's picture of sowing and reaping looks ahead to the next two psalms, which speak of work, family, and fruitfulness under God's hand (Psalms 127 and 128). It also gives the whole collection one of its most remembered promises.
historical:
The heading is simply “A song of ascents”. The phrase in verse 1 translated “restored the captives of Zion” has been read two ways. It can mean returning the captives, which points to the return from exile in Babylon after Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed deported peoples to go home (Ezra 1:1-4). It can also mean restoring fortunes more generally, since the same Hebrew idiom is used of Job's restored fortunes (Job 42:10), where no captivity was involved. On the first reading the psalm celebrates the return from exile; on the second it could celebrate any great reversal, such as Jerusalem's deliverance from the Assyrian army in 701 BC.

Most scholars read the psalm against the return from Babylon. That fits both halves: the joy of the return in verses 1-3, and the prayer for further restoration in verses 4-6, since the returned community faced crop failure, poverty, opposition, and a small and struggling temple (Haggai 1:5-11; Nehemiah 1:3). There is also a question of tense. Most translations read verses 1-3 as past, a memory of what God has done, but some read them as future, what it will be like when the LORD restores Zion. On that reading the whole psalm is hope rather than memory and hope.
cultural:
The Negev is the dry region in the south of Israel, running toward the Sinai. Its streambeds are dry most of the year, but when winter rains come the wadis can fill almost overnight and the desert turns green. To pray “Restore our captives, O LORD, like streams in the Negev” is to ask for sudden, total change, water where there was only dust.

Sowing and reaping were the rhythm of life for nearly everyone in ancient Israel. Sowing was hard and anxious: seed grain was a precious reserve that could otherwise be eaten, so throwing it on the ground was a costly act of hope, especially in years of hunger. The farmer walking out with seed in a bag, weeping, is a real picture of a poor year. Harvest was the season of joy, when sheaves were bound and carried in, and Israel's harvest festivals were marked by celebration (Deuteronomy 16:13-15). The psalm uses the most familiar experience in the land to say that sorrow sown in faith will not be wasted.
literary: Psalm 126 has two stanzas that mirror each other. Verses 1-3 remember a restoration, and verses 4-6 ask for one, and the same Hebrew phrase about restoring fortunes appears in verses 1 and 4 to link them. The first stanza builds with stair-step repetition: the nations say “The LORD has done great things for them”, and Israel answers, “The LORD has done great things for us”, turning the outsiders' words into its own confession. The second stanza moves from prayer (verse 4) to proverb (verse 5) to a small scene (verse 6), in which the contrasts are exact: going out and coming back, weeping and shouts of joy, a bag of seed and armfuls of sheaves. The word for joyful shouting (rinnah) appears three times, once in each part of the psalm.

outline.t: Remembering restoration: dreamers, laughter, great things
Prayer: restore us again, like streams in the Negev
Sowing in tears, reaping with joy

doctrines.note: The psalm holds memory and hope together. Because God has restored his people before, they can ask him to do it again, and they can sow in tears with the expectation of harvest.
Tears are not treated as a lack of faith. The one who goes out weeping is the one who comes back rejoicing; sorrow is the season in which the seed is sown.
The nations notice what God has done for Israel and say so. God's acts for his people are meant to be seen by the watching world, a theme that runs from the exodus to the prophets.

words.note: Rinnah, a ringing cry, usually of joy. It is loud, public, and physical, the shout of a harvest or a festival. Its three uses here (verses 2, 5, and 6) run through both halves of the psalm, from the remembered joy of restoration to the promised joy of harvest.

Shuv, to turn or return. Combined with a noun from a similar root, it forms the idiom translated here as restoring captives, which may mean bringing back exiles or reversing fortunes. The verb is also the Old Testament's main word for repentance, turning back to God. In verse 6 it describes the sower who will surely return with sheaves.

Chalam, to dream. The people say they were like dreamers, which can mean that the restoration felt unreal, too good to be true. Some interpreters connect it instead with a Hebrew root meaning to be healthy or strong, reading like those restored to health, and the ancient Greek translation has like those comforted. Either way, the line captures the dazed joy of sudden relief.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 126, but Jesus uses its pattern. He blesses those who weep now, saying they will laugh (Luke 6:21), and he tells his disciples that their sorrow will turn to joy, like a woman whose labor gives way to the birth of a child (John 16:20-22). He compares his own death to a grain of wheat that must fall into the ground and die in order to bear much fruit (John 12:24), which is sowing in tears on the largest scale. Paul uses the same agricultural logic for the resurrection of the body: what is sown perishable is raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42). The connection is thematic, but it runs deep: the restoration Israel celebrated and prayed for reaches its fullest form in the resurrection.

hard.q: If God already restored Zion, why do the people have to ask him to do it again?
hard.a: This is a real tension in the psalm, and it reflects the experience of the returned exiles. Coming home from Babylon was an astonishing gift, but it did not end their troubles: the land was poor, the rebuilt temple was modest, and they remained under foreign rule. Prophets like Haggai and Zechariah spoke of a greater restoration still to come. Some interpreters read the psalm as holding a partial fulfillment and a greater hope together. Others, reading verses 1-3 as future, see no tension at all, only a vision of the joy to come and a prayer for it. Either way, the psalm reflects a pattern found throughout Scripture: God acts decisively, and his people still wait for the full harvest of what he has begun.

questions: What is one restoration God has brought in your life that you look back on with the dazed joy of verse 1?
Where are you sowing in tears right now? What would it mean to keep sowing?
The nations saw what God did for Israel and spoke of it. What might people around you see of God's work in your life or your community?
